title: Touching and wudu
hook: schools differ on whether touching certain things breaks wudu

segments.voice: Yesterday, saying amin, and your line: aloud or silent. When you agreed with someone, did you say it out loud, or keep it to yourself? Day one thousand two hundred nine.

A couple heads out the door for the evening prayer. Both have just made wudu, the washing before prayer: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, feet. At the door, one reaches for the other's hand. Then a pause. Does that touch mean washing again before praying? Ask a Shafi'i teacher, a Hanafi teacher and a Maliki teacher, and you may get three different answers, each with a verse and a report behind it. It sounds like the smallest question in the world. It's actually a doorway into how the schools read one word. Today, touching and wudu.
screen: `FRESH WUDU, OUT THE DOOR.` → `ONE HAND REACHES FOR ANOTHER.` → `WASH AGAIN, OR NOT?`

segments.voice: First, the verse. In surah five, the Qur'an lists the things after which a believer who can't find water should use clean earth instead, and one of them is a phrase built on the verb lamasa: when you have touched women. The question is what touched means. Next, two readings. A report from Ibn Abbas takes the word as a polite way of naming intercourse, the way English says two people slept together. Others among the Companions, tradition says, took it as touch by hand. Hanafi scholars follow the first reading: a touch of the hand doesn't break wudu. They also point to Aisha's report in Sahih al-Bukhari: she lay in front of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ while he prayed at night, and when he went down to prostrate, he touched her feet so she would draw them in, and he kept praying. Then, the middle and the other end. Shafi'i scholars take touched as touch: skin on skin with an unrelated adult of the opposite sex breaks wudu, desire or not. Maliki and Hanbali scholars stand between: the touch breaks wudu when it comes with desire. Ja'fari jurists hold that touching doesn't break it at all. Last, a second case, with two reports side by side. Busra bint Safwan reports that whoever touches his private part should make wudu. Talq ibn Ali reports the Prophet asking, isn't it just a part of you? Shafi'is and Hanbalis lean on Busra; Hanafis on Talq. The details differ. The washing stays.
screen: `ONE VERB: LAMASA, TO TOUCH.` · `A POLITE WORD, OR A HAND?` · `SHAFI'I, MALIKI, HANBALI, JA'FARI.` · `BUSRA AND TALQ, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn your school's view, or simply notice your hands again. If you follow a school, ask yourself honestly whether you know what it teaches about touch and wudu, and make a note to ask someone who does. If you don't, recall one small rule you grew up with: shoes off at the door, no hat at the table, the first bite for the eldest. Do you know the reason behind it? Hold the rule for a few breaths, and the person who taught it to you. The bell holds the time.
Touching and wudu. Whether a touch breaks the washing before prayer: by one reading, it doesn't; by another, skin on skin does; by another, only with desire. Today's word.

Your line: details differ. Today, when a small rule surprises you, look for the reading behind it before you call it strange. Tomorrow, the night sky, and how a month begins. Day one thousand two hundred nine.

howItsDone: Each school teaches its own list of what breaks wudu: in the Shafi'i school skin contact with an unrelated adult of the opposite sex does, in the Maliki and Hanbali schools only touch with desire, and in the Hanafi and Ja'fari schools touch alone does not.

original.note: Arabic: touch; the verb lamasa stands behind the verse the schools read differently.

trapdoor: what you thought: wudu has one list of breakers everyone shares.
what it means: the schools share the core, and differ on details like touch, because they read one verb differently.
what a scholar hears: lamastum in surah 5:6 and 4:43, Ibn Abbas's reading, Aisha's report, and the hadith of Busra against the hadith of Talq.
